clue.text: Prayer leader: you can call me a leader of Muslims

parts.note: someone you can call 'a ...' would say "I'm a ..."

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, so only the start of the following word is kept

parts.note: first letter of Muslims

explanation.surface: A cleric introduces himself as the man who leads Muslim prayers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a self-introduction; read literally, 'you can call me a' is I'M A, and the leader of Muslims tops it off to give IMAM.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam is the person who leads the congregation in prayer at a mosque.

clue.text: Beer or punch?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for beer or other alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Someone at a party asks which drink to serve, ale or a fruit bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch looks like the drink, matching beer, but here it is the blow; wallop is old British slang for beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Wallop is both a slang noun for mild ale and an ordinary word for a hard hit.

clue.text: Rank individual numbers in pieces of music

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits within it, so the first item goes inside the second

parts.note: bars are short measured sections of a score
single units are ones

explanation.surface: Someone ranks particular tracks or movements on a playlist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' reads as a verb telling you to order the music, but it is the noun: a title in the peerage.
explanation.definitionFit: A baroness holds a title in the peerage, so the word names a rank of nobility.

clue.text: Strap yourself in and shut it!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fasten your seat belt
second meaning: a rude British way of saying be quiet

explanation.surface: A grumpy driver tells a passenger to put on the seat belt and stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are commands; the second sense is informal British for 'stop talking'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb literally means fasten a safety belt and colloquially means be quiet.

clue.text: Ultimately, innings do-or-die, unfortunately, for opener

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: last letter of innings

indicators.note: something gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters fall out of their order

parts.note: the letters of the hyphenated phrase

explanation.surface: A cricket report: in a desperate final innings things went badly for the opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener' and 'innings' paint cricket, where an opener is a batsman; here it is something that opens, a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A side door is a way into a building, so it can be called an opener in the cryptic sense of a thing that opens.

clue.text: Second wine down

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
rosé is a pink wine

explanation.surface: A second glass of wine is being knocked back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like the verb for drinking; it is the adjective meaning low in spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling down and being morose both describe a gloomy, sullen mood.

clue.text: Length of blade yet to turn up for saw

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up makes the letters climb, so they are read from bottom to top
a length of something is a stretch cut from it, so the letters come from a run of the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A carpenter waits for a piece of blade to appear in a saw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' wants to be the cutting tool next to 'blade'; it is the past tense of see.
explanation.definitionFit: To eye something is to look at it, so eyed is a past-tense synonym for saw.

clue.text: Limb almost entirely covered in cooked food served at breakfast

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped
something covered in another thing is wrapped by it, so the first group goes inside the second

parts.note: a meal that is made has been cooked
an arm is a limb
entirely means all; almost all loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A leg of meat is almost entirely smothered in a cooked breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked food' looks like one phrase, but 'cooked' belongs to the wordplay and the definition starts at 'food'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmalade is the citrus preserve spread on toast, a staple of the British breakfast table.

clue.text: Recording of communist bureaucracy

parts.note: red is the traditional label for a communist
a tape is a recording

explanation.surface: A recording made of a communist official's dealings with the state machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recording of communist' means the communist's recording, so the pieces go communist first.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is the idiom for excessive official rules and paperwork, which is bureaucracy.

clue.text: Climber pocketing gold key

indicators.note: pocketing something means putting it away inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: ivy is a climbing plant
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A mountaineer slips a golden key into a pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: The climber is a plant, not a mountaineer. OR in IVY.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano keys were traditionally made of ivory, so an ivory is informal for a key on a keyboard.

clue.text: Site of traffic island for pedestrian

definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally the centre of the carriageway, where a traffic island stands

explanation.surface: A traffic island is placed in the road to give walkers a refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' reads as a person on foot, fitting the traffic island; here it is the adjective meaning dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle-of-the-road describes moderate, unexciting views or tastes, which is pedestrian in its sense of ordinary.

clue.text: Nosh very good, feeding me pastry dish

indicators.note: feeding something means going into it as food goes into a mouth, so the first pieces sit inside the next

parts.note: taken as written
to nosh is to eat
pi is short for pious, very good

explanation.surface: Good food is being served to the speaker, a hearty pastry dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nosh' looks like a noun meaning food; it is the verb. PI for pious is a crossword standard.
explanation.definitionFit: A meat pie is a baked pastry case filled with meat, a classic savoury pastry dish.

clue.text: Suit and tie

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to go well with, as colours do
second meaning: a sporting fixture, as in a cup tie

explanation.walkthrough: Suit and tie paint an outfit; in fact suit is a verb and a tie is a game, as in a football cup tie.
explanation.definitionFit: Match is both a verb meaning to go together well and a noun meaning a contest between teams.

clue.text: Saying prayers initially, wanderer heading for basilica

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word before is kept

parts.note: first letter of prayers
a rover is someone who wanders

indicators.note: a heading is what sits on top, so the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: first letter of basilica

explanation.surface: A pilgrim says prayers on the way into a great church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saying' reads as a verb about praying; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverb is a short traditional saying expressing a general truth.

clue.text: By the sound of it, committee nodding off?

indicators.note: this phrase asks us to judge by what we hear, not how a word is written

parts.note: a board is a governing committee

explanation.surface: A dull committee meeting where members are falling asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as a loose example: being bored can make you nod off.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone nodding off is likely weary from tedium, so bored stands for that state by example.

clue.text: Falling apart after row, her woes compounded

indicators.note: compounded means mixed together, so the letters are combined in a new order

parts.note: all fifteen letters of these words

explanation.surface: After an argument, a woman's troubles pile up and she goes to pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The worse for wear is an idiom for being damaged, worn out or in poor condition, so falling apart.

clue.text: Clear away one side

parts.note: someone away from home is out
right is one of the two sides

explanation.surface: An instruction to push one side of something away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like a verb of tidying; it is the adjective meaning unambiguous.
explanation.definitionFit: An outright winner is a clear one, with no doubt about the result.

clue.text: Safer net designed for catch, say?

indicators.note: something designed is newly arranged, so these letters are laid out differently

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A better safety net has been built for catching falling acrobats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' suggests catching someone in a net; it is the noun for a clasp, given as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch on a door or bag is one example of a fastener, a device that holds things shut.

clue.text: Old money? Discuss at length

parts.note: ex means former, old
the pound is British money

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to talk at length about old currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old money' looks like one phrase for pre-decimal coins; the two words act separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound is to set out and explain a subject in detail, which means discussing it at length.

clue.text: Label dish with game

parts.note: hash is a dish of chopped meat and potato
tag is a children's chasing game

explanation.surface: A menu labels a dish as containing game meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like the meat; it is the playground game.
explanation.definitionFit: A hashtag is a word prefixed with # used to label social media posts by topic.

clue.text: Flighty animal in house of swine

indicators.note: something in a house is inside it, so the first item goes within the dwelling named

parts.note: a sty is where pigs live
a cat is an animal

explanation.surface: A skittish creature has got into the pigs' home.
explanation.walkthrough: The house of swine is a sty.
explanation.definitionFit: Scatty is British informal for scatterbrained and disorganised, the same as flighty.

clue.text: Retriever, say, set free in outskirts of Godalming

indicators.note: one thing set in another is placed inside it
the outskirts are the edges of a place, so only the first and last letters are used

parts.note: first and last letters of Godalming, a town in Surrey
to undo a knot or tether sets something free

explanation.surface: A dog is let off its lead on the edge of a Surrey town.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example, flagged by 'say'; Godalming is a market town in Surrey, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrievers are bred to fetch shot game, so a retriever is one kind of gun dog.

clue.text: Pride scattering by the way — as tiger appears

parts.note: St is short for street, a way

indicators.note: scattering throws things about, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: the letters of the word

explanation.surface: A pride of lions flees at the roadside when a tiger shows up.
explanation.walkthrough: A pride is a group of lions, which helps the big-cat picture; 'by' places ST beside the shuffled word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiger's coat is marked with dark stripes, so striped describes how it looks.

clue.text: Stuffed sheep taken over sea

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing taken over another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A stuffed sheep is shipped across the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffed' reads as taxidermy; it is the verb for packing tightly.
explanation.definitionFit: To ram something in is to force or cram it in, so rammed means stuffed.

clue.text: Tragically ma, in truth, I love a drink!

indicators.note: things that go tragically have gone badly wrong, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: the letters of these words
taken as written, before it doubles as the start of the definition

explanation.surface: A sad confession: Mother really does love a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' does double duty, finishing the fodder and opening the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian vermouth is sweet red vermouth, a fortified wine drunk as an aperitif or in cocktails.

clue.text: English isle over a US state

indicators.note: in a down clue the item over another is written above it, so it comes first

parts.note: IOW is short for the Isle of Wight, an island off southern England
taken as written

explanation.surface: An English island set against an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Wight lies off the south coast of England and is often abbreviated IOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Iowa is a Midwestern state of the USA.

clue.text: Some patch I described for mask

indicators.note: some means only part, so the letters lie within the words that follow

parts.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A writer describes a patch worn as a mask.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from the end of patch through I into the start of described.
explanation.definitionFit: To mask something is to conceal it, so hide is a verb synonym.

clue.text: Stand guard over timer

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a timepiece worn on the wrist

explanation.surface: Someone is told to guard a clock or stopwatch.
explanation.definitionFit: Watch is a verb for keeping vigil and a noun for a small portable timepiece.

clue.text: With lid removed, finished fluid

parts.note: a container with its lid off is open
something finished has ended

explanation.surface: A jar with its lid off has spilled its liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fluid' looks like a liquid noun; it is the adjective meaning flexible.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-ended arrangement is flexible with no fixed limit, which is fluid in the sense of changeable.
